LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Thymus:
Overview — The T-Cell School

The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ — the site where T cells mature and are “educated”. It is a bilobed organ in the anterior mediastinum, largest at puberty, after which it involutes and is replaced by fat.

🔬 Image slot — thymus at low power — lobules with a dark T-cell-rich cortex, a pale medulla, and Hassall's corpuscles

It develops from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch: an epithelial framework (from endoderm) colonised by lymphoid cells (from bone marrow).

Unlike a lymph node, the thymus has no B-cell follicles, no germinal centres and no afferent lymphatics — it is a T-cell factory, not a filter.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — thymic lobule — densely packed cortical thymocytes, a paler medulla, and a concentric keratinised Hassall's corpuscle
  • Lobules with an outer dark cortex (densely packed thymocytes) and an inner pale medulla.
  • Hassall’s (thymic) corpuscles in the medulla — concentric whorls of keratinised epithelial cells — the diagnostic feature.
  • No lymphoid follicles or germinal centres (contrast with lymph node/spleen).
Dark cortex + pale medulla + Hassall’s corpuscles → thymus. Hassall’s corpuscles alone clinch it — nothing else in the body looks like them.
Cortex, Medulla & Hassall’s Corpuscles
Cortex (dark)
  • Densely packed immature thymocytes (T cells)
  • Contains the blood–thymus barrier
  • Site of positive selection
Medulla (pale)
  • Fewer, more mature T cells
  • Contains Hassall’s corpuscles
  • Site of negative selection
  • Hassall’s corpuscles are concentric, keratinised aggregates of epithelial reticular cells; they increase with age and help regulate T-cell development.
The cortex is dark because it is crammed with maturing thymocytes; the medulla is pale. Hassall’s corpuscles mark the medulla.
Epithelial Reticular Cells & T-Cell Selection
🔬 Image slot — T-cell selection — positive selection in the cortex (recognise self-MHC) and negative selection in the medulla (delete self-reactive cells)
  • Epithelial reticular cells form the supporting framework (not reticular fibres), make thymic hormones (thymosin, thymopoietin), build the blood–thymus barrier, and present MHC for T-cell selection.
1
Positive selection (cortex)keep T cells that recognise self-MHC
2
Negative selection (medulla)delete T cells strongly reactive to self-antigen
3
Central toleranceonly self-tolerant, MHC-restricted T cells leave
Medullary cells use the AIRE gene to display peripheral self-antigens for negative selection. AIRE mutation → multi-organ autoimmunity (APECED).
Age Involution
  • The thymus is largest at puberty, then progressively involutes: thymic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue and thymocyte numbers fall.
  • T-cell output declines with age, but the peripheral T-cell pool is already established.
Age involution (fatty replacement) is normal; do not mistake a fatty adult thymus for pathology.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
DiGeorge syndrome
22q11 deletion → thymic aplasia/hypoplasia → T-cell immunodeficiency (+ hypocalcaemia, cardiac defects)
Thymoma
Epithelial tumour; associated with myasthenia gravis, pure red-cell aplasia & hypogammaglobulinaemia
Myasthenia gravis
Thymic hyperplasia or thymoma; anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies; may improve after thymectomy
SCID
Severe combined immunodeficiency — failure of T-cell (± B-cell) development
APECED (AIRE mutation)
Failed negative selection → autoimmune polyendocrinopathy
Thymic (follicular) hyperplasia
Germinal centres appear in the medulla — associated with autoimmune disease
⭐ Exam Pearls
Dark cortex + pale medulla + Hassall’s corpuscles = thymus.
Hassall’s corpuscles (medulla) = diagnostic: concentric keratinised epithelial cells.
Primary lymphoid organ for T-cell maturation — no B follicles, germinal centres or afferent lymphatics.
Positive selection = cortex (recognise self-MHC); negative selection = medulla (delete self-reactive; AIRE).
Epithelial reticular cells form the framework + blood–thymus barrier + thymic hormones (thymosin).
Largest at puberty, then involutes (replaced by fat) — a normal change.
DiGeorge (22q11) = thymic aplasia → T-cell deficiency; thymoma → myasthenia gravis.
AIRE mutation → failed negative selection → APECED autoimmunity.
LYMPHOID / IMMUNE__Lymph Node:
Overview — The Lymph Filter & Immune Hub

The lymph node is a secondary lymphoid organ: it filters lymph and is where adaptive immune responses are generated (antigen presentation, B- and T-cell activation). It is a bean-shaped, encapsulated organ arranged in three zones.

🔬 Image slot — lymph node at low power — capsule, subcapsular sinus, cortex with follicles, deep paracortex, and central medulla with a hilum
1
CortexB-cell follicles
2
ParacortexT cells + high endothelial venules
3
Medullamedullary cords (plasma cells) + sinuses
Learn it as a map: B cells in the cortical follicles, T cells in the paracortex, plasma cells in the medulla — and lymph flowing through sinuses from surface to hilum.
How to Recognise It on a Slide ⭐
🔬 Image slot — lymph node cortex — capsule, subcapsular sinus, and a secondary follicle with a pale germinal centre and dark mantle zone
  • A dense connective-tissue capsule with a subcapsular sinus beneath it.
  • Cortical follicles — rounded B-cell aggregates, often with pale germinal centres.
  • A diffuse paracortex (T cells) and a central medulla of cords and sinuses.
Capsule + subcapsular sinus + cortical follicles + paracortex + medulla → lymph node. A germinal centre with a “starry-sky” look confirms an active B-cell response.
Cortex, Paracortex & Medulla
Cortex (follicles)
B cells; primary follicles (no germinal centre) vs secondary follicles (active germinal centre + mantle zone)
Paracortex (deep cortex)
T cells + high endothelial venules (HEVs) where lymphocytes enter from blood; interdigitating dendritic cells
Medulla
Medullary cords (plasma cells, B cells, macrophages) between medullary sinuses
B-cortex, T-paracortex, plasma-cell medulla. The paracortex expands in viral infection (T-cell response); the follicles expand in B-cell responses.
Lymph Flow & the Sinus System
🔬 Image slot — lymph flow — multiple afferent lymphatics on the convex surface, through subcapsular and medullary sinuses, to a single efferent vessel at the hilum
1
Afferent lymphaticsmany, on the convex surface
2
Subcapsular → trabecular → medullary sinusesmacrophages filter antigen/debris
3
Efferent lymphaticsingle, leaves at the hilum
  • Many afferents in, one efferent out — and valves keep flow one-way; the artery and vein enter/leave at the hilum.
  • HEVs in the paracortex are the entry point for blood-borne lymphocytes recirculating into the node.
Because lymph enters through the subcapsular sinus, metastatic tumour cells seed the subcapsular sinus first — a key staging fact.
The Germinal Centre & Reactive Patterns
  • A germinal centre (secondary follicle) is a site of B-cell proliferation, somatic hypermutation and affinity maturation, supported by follicular dendritic cells.
  • Tingible-body macrophages clearing apoptotic B cells give the “starry-sky” appearance.
  • Output: high-affinity plasma cells (to the medulla) and memory B cells.
Follicular hyperplasia
  • B-cell response (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, early HIV)
Paracortical hyperplasia
  • T-cell response (viral infections, drug reactions)
Reactive follicular hyperplasia keeps a preserved architecture & polarised germinal centres with tingible-body macrophages — features that help distinguish it from follicular lymphoma.
Clinical / Pathological Correlate
Reactive lymphadenopathy
Follicular (B), paracortical (viral/drug) or sinus histiocytosis patterns; architecture preserved
Hodgkin lymphoma
Reed–Sternberg cells (“owl-eye”, CD15/CD30+); orderly contiguous spread
Follicular lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin B-cell; t(14;18) overexpressing BCL2; back-to-back follicles
Burkitt lymphoma
t(8;14) MYC; very high turnover with a “starry-sky” pattern
Metastatic carcinoma
Seeds the subcapsular sinus first; basis of sentinel-node biopsy
Granulomatous lymphadenitis
Caseating (TB) vs non-caseating (sarcoidosis) granulomas
Loss of the normal nodal architecture (effacement) by a monotonous cell population points to lymphoma rather than reactive change.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Capsule + subcapsular sinus + cortical follicles + paracortex + medulla = lymph node.
B-cortex (follicles), T-paracortex (+ HEVs), plasma-cell medulla.
Germinal centre = active B-cell response; tingible-body macrophages give the starry sky.
HEVs in the paracortex are where blood lymphocytes enter the node.
Lymph flow: many afferents (convex) → sinuses → one efferent (hilum); valves keep it one-way.
Metastases seed the subcapsular sinus first (sentinel node principle).
Follicular hyperplasia = B (RA, HIV); paracortical hyperplasia = T (viral/drug).
Reed–Sternberg = Hodgkin; follicular lymphoma t(14;18)/BCL2; Burkitt t(8;14)/MYC starry sky.
